title: The space between
line: What becomes possible is between the parts
narration:
We spend a lot of time looking at the most powerful thing in the picture.
The biggest machine. The fastest chip. The most capable model.

Tonight I'd like to spend some time looking between them.

Because the next question for enterprise AI is what happens when it has to
work with everything else. When it needs an answer from another system,
permission from another organization, or evidence that something actually
happened.

line: The network is the computer.
narration:
John Gage gave us a sentence many people in this room know well.

It asks us to think about the capability of the connected system.
What becomes available when computation, information, and people can reach
one another?

AI gives that question a new urgency. We are beginning to ask software
to decide what to do across the systems we connected.

title: The people who join it up
line: Different systems. Different knowledge. One operation.
narration:
People make this work every day. Dispatchers, planners, crews, and the
person who answers when a customer asks where the shipment is.

They work across systems that each know something useful. The aircraft
system knows capacity. The hub knows its processing window. The delivery
system knows the destination commitment.

Someone has to bring those answers together into a decision.

title: Give the network a purpose
line:
Tokyo → Boston
A promise to someone waiting.
narration:
For this example, the shipment has a promised arrival time and a handling
limit. Its contents are sensitive to shock.

Those two conditions give the operation a purpose. Arriving on time with
damaged cargo would still fail the customer.

The enterprise is full of commitments like this. Its equipment, software,
and people have to work together to keep them.
visualChange: Keep V2’s enterprise dependencies and arrival/handling promise. Use V1’s recognizable aircraft silhouette for the aircraft carrying Shipment TK–BOS / 01. Each reveal is a manual stop.

title: The plan stops working
line: The gateway closes.
narration:
Weather closes a gateway on the planned route.

The servers can still be running. The network can still be carrying traffic.
The aircraft can still be serviceable.

But the plan we made for this shipment no longer works. We have to find
another way to keep the promise.
visualChange: Keep V2’s enterprise dependencies and arrival/handling promise. Use V1’s recognizable aircraft silhouette for the aircraft carrying Shipment TK–BOS / 01. Each reveal is a manual stop.

title: Healthy systems, endangered outcome
line:
The systems are healthy.
The promise is at risk.
narration:
This is a familiar gap for an IT organization.

We can have an accurate picture of component health and still need another
view to understand the business consequence. Which shipments depend on
that connection? Which commitments are now in danger? How much time is left
to change the plan?

The answers sit in the relationships between the systems.
visualChange: Keep V2’s enterprise dependencies and arrival/handling promise. Use V1’s recognizable aircraft silhouette for the aircraft carrying Shipment TK–BOS / 01. Each reveal is a manual stop.

title: Follow the consequence
line: What depends on this connection?
narration:
The gateway closure matters because it changes the next connection.
That changes the sorting window. That can change the final delivery.

A dispatcher follows those dependencies and looks for an alternative
that still fits. Available space on another aircraft is useful only if
the next hub can receive it and the shipment can still reach the customer.

This is the difference between finding capacity and finding a workable plan.
visualChange: Keep V2’s enterprise dependencies and arrival/handling promise. Use V1’s recognizable aircraft silhouette for the aircraft carrying Shipment TK–BOS / 01. Each reveal is a manual stop.

title: Awaiting confirmation

visualChange: Keep V2’s enterprise dependencies and arrival/handling promise. Use V1’s recognizable aircraft silhouette for the aircraft carrying Shipment TK–BOS / 01. Each reveal is a manual stop.

title: The answer returns

visualChange: Keep V2’s enterprise dependencies and arrival/handling promise. Use V1’s recognizable aircraft silhouette for the aircraft carrying Shipment TK–BOS / 01. Each reveal is a manual stop.

title: The promise survives
line: A different route. The same commitment.
narration:
She changes the route, and the revised plan still meets the commitment.

Her judgment matters. So does her ability to reach the people and systems
that know whether the plan can work.

If we want an agent to help with more of that work, we have to give it a
usable understanding of these relationships and a reliable way to check
what is true now.

title: What the agent needs to understand
line: A model of what depends on what.
narration:
This is the model I mean: a representation of the operation that connects
its resources, dependencies, current state, commitments, and permissions.

For this shipment, it links the package to the aircraft, the aircraft to
the receiving hub, and those movements to an arrival promise.

That gives a reasoner something concrete to work with. It can ask how a
change in one place affects an outcome somewhere else.
visualChange: Keep V2’s enterprise dependencies and arrival/handling promise. Use V1’s recognizable aircraft silhouette for the aircraft carrying Shipment TK–BOS / 01. Each reveal is a manual stop.

title: Facts, promises, permission
line:
What is true?
What is promised?
What is allowed?
narration:
Those are different kinds of information.

An aircraft has available capacity. That's a fact to verify. The shipment
has an arrival commitment. That's an outcome to protect. The agent may
be allowed to reserve space, but not to change the customer's terms.
That's an authority boundary.

A useful enterprise model preserves those distinctions. Otherwise a
plausible plan can quietly assume a permission it was never given.
visualChange: Keep V2’s enterprise dependencies and arrival/handling promise. Use V1’s recognizable aircraft silhouette for the aircraft carrying Shipment TK–BOS / 01. Each reveal is a manual stop.

title: Ask the source
line: Connected knowledge. Accountable sources.
narration:
The knowledge is distributed. The aircraft system owns one answer.
The hub owns another. A customer agreement supplies a different constraint.

We can bring those together without pretending that one copy is always
current. Some information can be stored. Some needs refreshing. Some has
to be checked at the moment of commitment.

The model needs to preserve where an answer came from, how current it is,
and who has authority over it.
visualChange: Keep V2’s enterprise dependencies and arrival/handling promise. Use V1’s recognizable aircraft silhouette for the aircraft carrying Shipment TK–BOS / 01. Each reveal is a manual stop.

title: The title's second meaning
line: A model of the enterprise gives reasoning something to work with.
narration:
When we say “the model” in an AI conversation, we usually mean the trained
model doing the reasoning.

There is another model we need to care about: its representation of the
enterprise it is being asked to operate.

The quality of the reasoner matters. So does the quality of what it knows
about this business, and its ability to check that knowledge as the business
changes. Better reasoning cannot manufacture missing authority or current
capacity.

title: Delegate a defined job
line: One agent. A defined job.
narration:
We give the operations agent a job: evaluate a route change for this shipment and submit it when the required checks and approvals are satisfied.

The job has an outcome, a deadline, and limits on what the agent can authorize. Flight operations and the relevant authorities retain their responsibilities.

Delivering the shipment involves many jobs. This agent is responsible for one bounded part of that work: putting a workable, authorized route decision through the systems that have to carry it out.

title: New evidence
line: The plan meets new evidence.
narration:
The planned route was acceptable on the information available when it was
chosen. Now an aircraft ahead reports a rougher ride.

The agent needs to establish whether that report is relevant to our path,
recent enough to use, and significant for this cargo's handling limit.

A newer report deserves attention. It still needs context. The question
is whether the evidence changes what this shipment can safely tolerate.

title: A proposal is not a commitment
line: An alternative must satisfy the whole journey.
narration:
An alternative might reduce the exposure. It can also change arrival time,
fuel requirements, or the approvals needed to use the route.

Those checks belong to the systems and authorities responsible for them.
The agent has to obtain their answers and establish that the candidate
still fits the shipment's commitments.

Finding an appealing alternative is the beginning of the decision.

title: Open the workload
line: One job creates a distributed workload.
narration:
Now open up that job. The agent consults models, requests weather evidence, checks capacity and arrival windows, and seeks approval. It also needs acceptance from the system that records the amendment.

All the processing and traffic associated with carrying out the job is its workload. That includes reasoning, checks, retries, and feedback.

Map that workload, and you see the nodes and connections that have to work together. Processing happens at the nodes. Exchanges carry the work between them.

title: The job has a deadline
line: Can the workload complete in time?
narration:
An answer can be correct and too late. The workload has to complete the required checks and exchanges within the job’s decision window.

If the opportunity to use the route has passed, a successful response does not recover it. We need to measure against the time the job actually has available.

When that time runs out, hold the commitment, continue on an approved plan where appropriate, or bring a person in. The response cannot be to silently assume success.

title: The uncertain acknowledgment
line: Did it fail—or did the acknowledgment fail?

There's another problem worth preparing for before we submit anything.
The receiving system may accept a change and the acknowledgment may never
get back to us.

From the sender's side, that can look like failure. Sending the same
instruction again as a new transaction can create a duplicate commitment.

We need to resolve what happened without accidentally doing it twice.

A retry adds activity to the workload. It must preserve the identity of the intended change.

The sender and receiver need an agreed way to recognize the same operation, look up its status, and handle a repeated request safely. That lets the agent recover an answer without creating another commitment.

A job can involve several transactions. A genuinely new route decision needs its own evidence, authority, and record. The identity of the job does not make every operation inside it the same operation.

title: Many jobs share capacity
line: Many agents. Many jobs. Shared capacity.
narration:
Now add the other flights responding to the same weather event. Each agent has a job, and each job creates a workload.

Their agents can all be acting reasonably and still overwhelm a shared service together. The critical processing and exchanges for our job need a way to meet their deadline under that load.

That may require admission control, reserved capacity, or workload isolation across the service path. A dedicated-looking line on a diagram does not help if every request still waits in the same overloaded queue.

title: The workload crosses boundaries

Another provider may supply weather. It cannot substitute for the authority that has to approve the route.

title: Keep learning from the operation
line: The next decision starts with the latest result.
narration:
The operation continues. Conditions can change again. New observations
update the picture available for the next decision.

The same commitment should survive a retry. A new situation can require
a new decision.

That is why sensing and verification have to remain connected to action
throughout the work. We are operating in a changing environment.

What looked like one job for one agent required coordinated work across all these nodes. This is the workload mapped onto the network.

The aircraft and shipment are the same ones we started with. Weather evidence, operational constraints, models, approval, and the system recording the amendment all participated. Flight operations and measurements then told us what actually happened.

The applications participated in the job. Their individual operations contributed to its workload. The connected system made the coordination possible.

title: The workload spans compute and connections

Pull back again. The same job draws on an ecosystem of companies and systems: weather providers, model providers, the logistics company, its airline partner, and the ground operation.

Under the models are serving clusters, compute fabrics, and chips. Between the companies are wide area networks and interconnects. Processing at the nodes and traffic between them together make up the workload.

One job can span many applications. Many jobs can share the same nodes and connections. This is the full system we are asking to behave intelligently.

title: Design connectivity around the job
line: Design connectivity around the job.
narration:
Designing the job means deciding which nodes can participate, what context they exchange, how long they can wait, and how they recover when an answer does not arrive. Who is allowed to act? Which systems must agree before the work can proceed?

We have to express those choices in the software coordinating the workload. Reachability, deadlines, retries, and authorization shape whether the agent can complete its job.

The network of exchanges is a core part of the intelligent system. Information has to reach the right place, in time for effective reasoning and coordinated action.

title: Observe the workload, verify the outcome
line: Observe the workload. Verify the outcome.
narration:
Build observability across the workload. Connect the processing and exchanges to the job they serve: which evidence was used, what conditions held, what action was authorized, and what the operation reports happened.

The aircraft’s measurements, the cargo monitor, the arrival report, and the health of the communication path all feed that picture. Completing a call does not establish that the job succeeded. Completing the agent’s route-change job does not by itself establish that the delivery promise was kept.

This is situational awareness: understanding the conditions in which a decision is made, then sensing and understanding its outcome. That feedback informs the next decision, within delegated limits. Which brings us to who sets those limits.

People decide what can be delegated, which risks are acceptable, and when

That responsibility doesn't disappear as routine work becomes more
autonomous. It becomes part of how we design and run the operation.

People keep the right to say what the round trip is for.
